Stage 3 · Grammar

How a story is built — and how you answer one

No new tenses. You already have both. Today they work together, with the phrases around them.

Read the opening of one of today’s stories.
  • A funny thing happened this morning.
  • I was on the train and there was a young woman sitting opposite me.
  • So, anyway, I was feeling a bit thirsty, so I got some juice out of my bag.
  • Suddenly the straw jumped out of my mouth and the juice landed on her white shirt!
Which tense sets the scene, and which one moves the story on?
The shape of a spoken story
PartWhat it doesLanguage
1 · Open itTell them a story is comingYou’ll never believe what happened… · A funny thing happened this morning. · I had a bad experience last year.
2 · Set the sceneWhere, when, what was going on Past ContinuousI was having lunch with a friend… · The sun was shining and I was looking out of the window.
3 · Move it onThe events, in order Past SimpleSo, anyway, a man came over… · Then the pilot made an announcement.
4 · The momentThe two tenses togetherThe wheels were just touching the ground when the plane took off again.
5 · Say how you feltThe reaction of the tellerI was so embarrassed! · I was really scared! · I was so angry!
6 · Close itLand the endingIn the end it was all OK. · What a nightmare!
The listener has a job too
  • Oh no! — something bad has just happened
  • Really? · That’s strange! — keep them going
  • You’re joking! — you can hardly believe it
  • That’s awful! · That’s terrible! — sympathy
  • What a nightmare! — the whole thing was a disaster
  • So then what happened? — ask for the next part
Where to use them
  • A story with a silent listener stops dead. React at least three times.
  • Reactions are short. One or two words is normal.
  • So then what happened? is the one that keeps a long story moving.
  • In writing you use the same phrases, plus Guess what and Anyway.

THE TWO TENSES. Past Continuous is the background; Past Simple is the event. You met both in Lessons 7 and 8 — today they sit in the same story.

OPENERS AND LINKERS. You’ll never believe what happened starts it; So, anyway moves it on; In the end closes it.

REACTIONS. Short, fast and frequent. The listener is half of the conversation.

A story told entirely in the Past Simple sounds like a list. Set the scene first.

The Unit 3 Test comes after this lesson.

THE TWO TENSES TOGETHER. Nothing here is new. The Past Continuous, from Lesson 8, paints the background: where you were, what was going on, what the weather was doing. The Past Simple, from Lesson 7, delivers the events one after another. A good spoken story almost always opens with a line or two of background and then switches to the simple form and stays there: I was having lunch with a friend in a café when a man came over and asked for directions.

OPENING. English speakers warn you that a story is coming: You’ll never believe what happened… · A funny thing happened this morning. · I had a bad experience last year. Without an opener, the listener does not know to start listening.

MOVING IT ON. So, anyway is the workhorse. It signals ‘background over, here comes the point’, and it appears in both of today’s recordings. Then and A few minutes later do the same job inside the sequence, and In the end closes it.

REACTING. This is the half that learners skip, and it is the half that makes a conversation sound real. The phrases are short and there are only about six you need: Oh no! · Really? · You’re joking! · That’s awful! · What a nightmare! · So then what happened? Listen to the café conversation in Stage 5 and count how often the listener speaks — it is far more often than most learners expect.

IN WRITING. An informal email uses the same story shape and most of the same phrases, plus a few that belong to letters: Dear…, Guess what, Anyway, Write back soon. You will see all of them in the model in Stage 6.

Two things to avoid: a story told entirely in the Past Simple, which sounds like a shopping list; and a listener who says nothing, which makes the teller stop.

This is the last lesson of Unit 3. The Unit Test covers Past Simple, Past Continuous and the adverbs of manner from Lesson 8.

Full grammar reference — Telling a story, and reacting to one

Form

The framePast Continuous sets the scene → Past Simple carries the events
OpeningYou’ll never believe what happened…
Sequencingfirst · then · after that · suddenly · in the end
ReactingThat’s awful! · What a nightmare! · Really? · You’re joking!
Keeping it goingSo what did you do? · And then?

When and why we use it

  • Open with a hook so the listener knows a story is coming.
  • Set the scene in the Past Continuous, then move to the Past Simple and stay there.
  • React with a short phrase and then a question — that is what keeps a conversation alive.
  • Close the story clearly: In the end, we took a taxi.

Signal words

anyway · so · in the end · luckily · unfortunately

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • At the end we took a taxi. → In the end we took a taxi.At the end = position; in the end = finally.
  • It’s a pity for you. → That’s a shame.Fixed reaction phrase.
  • I was losing my passport. → I lost my passport.A single event, not a background action.
  • What a nightmare it is! → What a nightmare!The phrase is fixed — nothing follows it.

Don’t confuse it with

That’s awful answers bad news; That’s fantastic answers good news. Do not use It’s interesting for either — it sounds cold.

Stage 6 · The model

The email you send afterwards

The same story shape, written down.

Read the whole email once. Do not do anything else yet.

An informal email

Dear Aisha,

Guess what happened to me on Saturday! You’ll never believe it.

I was going to my cousin’s wedding in Almaty, so I took the early train. Everything was fine for about two hours. I was reading and drinking coffee when the train suddenly stopped in the middle of nowhere. Nobody told us anything for forty minutes.

Then the guard came through and said there was a problem with the line. We had to get off and wait for a bus. It was raining, of course, and I was wearing my wedding clothes!

Anyway, the bus finally came and we arrived four hours late. I walked into the restaurant while everybody was eating dessert. My aunt just looked at me and laughed.

In the end it was fine — they gave me a plate of food and my cousin said it was the best entrance of the day. What a nightmare, though!

Write back soon and tell me about your week.

Love,
Dana

The shape to copy
  • Dear + first name
  • Guess what / You’ll never believe — the news is coming
  • Set the scene — where you were, what you were doing
  • The events — Past Simple, in order, with one when or while sentence
  • Anyway — move to the last part
  • In the end — how it finished
  • Write back soon + Love / Best wishes
Stage 7 · Now you

Tell it, react to it, write it

Your own worst journey — out loud first, then on paper.

Useful language

You’ll never believe what happened…  I was …ing when…  So, anyway…  In the end…

Oh no!  Really?  You’re joking!  That’s awful!  What a nightmare!  So then what happened?

Teller: use an opener, one when or while sentence, and a closing line. Listener: react at least three times.

Work in pairs. Choose a card, tell the story, then swap roles.
Choose a card and plan the story you will write.
Card A

The worst journey you have had. Where were you going? What were you doing when it went wrong? How did it end?

Card B

Round 1. A tells, B reacts at least three times and asks So then what happened? once.

Round 2. Swap. The listener’s job is half the task — a silent listener stops the story.

Now write the email.
Write it

Write an informal email to a friend about the same story. 120–150 words. Follow the shape from Stage 6: Dear → Guess what → the scene → the events → Anyway → In the end → Write back soon.

Check your email against five things: an opener, at least one Past Continuous scene sentence, one when or while sentence, In the end, and an informal sign-off.
